questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of Meigs syndrome?

explanation.text: Dysgerminoma is a type of germ cell tumour and is not part of Meigs syndrome. Meigs Syndrome: Meigs syndrome is a condition characterised by a triad of: Ovarian fibroma (fibrothecoma) Ascites Hydrothorax (pleural effusion)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is accurate concerning liquid-based cytology?

options.C: Study of fluid in the tumor microenvironment

explanation.text: Liquid-based cytology is often used to collect specimens, including urine, and study cells for various diagnostic purposes. Liquid-based cytology: It is a technique to collect and prepare cell samples for microscopic analysis. It involves gathering cells from various body fluids, such as cervical or vaginal fluids, respiratory secretions, or urine, depending on the diagnostic goal. This method is commonly used for cervical cancer screening.

Cells collected from the cervix with a brush or spatula are suspended in a preservative solution. This suspension is used to prepare slides for cytological examination to detect abnormalities or disease. Advantages of Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC): Improved slide preparation: LBC creates a thin-layer or monolayer slide preparation, providing better quality and clarity than conventional Papanicolaou (Pap) smears.

Enhanced cell preservation: The collection fluid used in LBC fixes, homogenizes, and rinses the cells, ensuring better preservation for microscopic examination. Reduced sample contamination: The homogenization process minimizes the presence of non-representative material, such as blood or mucus, leading to a more accurate analysis of the collected cells.

Increased diagnostic accuracy: With improved sample quality, LBC enhances the sensitivity and specificity of cervical cancer screening, allowing for more reliable detection of abnormalities. Disadvantage: Although cervical cytological screening has proven effective in reducing the incidence and mortality of cervical cancer, the conventional Pap test is less sensitive than commonly thought.
The false-negative rate of the conventional Pap test has been reported to reach as high as 50%.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a constituent of the Papanicolaou stain?

explanation.text: Eosin B is not a constituent of the Papanicolaou stain. Eosin is a different type of stain typically used for general histology to highlight cytoplasm in tissues, but it is not used in the Papanicolaou (Pap) stain. The Papanicolaou (Pap) stain is a widely used technique for examining cells from the cervix to screen for cervical cancer and other abnormalities.

It uses a combination of multiple dyes to differentiate cellular components: Hematoxylin - Stains the cell nuclei, allowing for clear visualization of nuclear structure. Orange G - Stains keratinized cells orange, highlighting squamous cells. Eosin A - Second counterstain & a polychrome mixture of Eosin Y and Light Green (stains cytoplasm and helps differentiate between various cell types).

questions.question: A patient presents with ascites and omental caking. Imaging reveals solid components in an adnexal mass, and there is a long-standing history of symptoms. CA-125 is positive. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanation.text: The presence of ascites, omental caking, a solid adnexal mass, elevated CA-125, and chronic vague symptoms strongly points to serous ovarian tumor. Types of Epithelial Ovarian Tumor: Type of Epithelial Ovarian Tumor Characteristics Clinical Presentation Serous Tumors Serous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, cystic spaces with serous epithelium. Large cystic mass, unilateral.

Serous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, often bilateral, cystic and solid components. Bilateral involvement in 30%, elevated CA-125. Mucinous Tumors Mucinous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, filled with mucinous fluid. Large, unilateral mass. Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, unilateral, mucinous epithelial lining. May rupture and spread to the peritoneum.

**Endometrioid Tumors (Option C ruled out):** Endometrioid Carcinoma: Arises from endometrial-like tissue, solid and cystic. Solid and cystic components, associated with endometriosis. Clear Cell Tumors Clear Cell Carcinoma: Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen accumulation. Advanced stage, associated with endometriosis. Brenner Tumors (Transitional Cell) Brenner Tumor: Transitional epithelial cells resembling urinary tract epithelium. Rare, usually benign.

**Mucinous ovarian tumor (Option B):** typically presents as a large, unilateral, multiloculated cystic mass and is less commonly associated with peritoneal spread or omental caking. CA-125 elevation is not as prominent unless the disease is advanced, and it lacks the classic imaging and spread pattern seen in serous carcinoma.

**Granulosa cell tumors (Option D):** are sex cord-stromal tumors that secrete estrogen and often cause hormonal symptoms like abnormal uterine bleeding; they rarely cause ascites or omental caking, and CA-125 is typically not elevated.

questions.question: A histopathological image of an ovarian mass in a lady is shown below. Which of the following statements are true regarding this condition? Sex cord stromal tumor Call-Exner bodies are seen CA125 is high Inhibin is a marker

explanation.text: The ovarian tumor showing Call-Exner bodies on histopathology is most consistent with a Granulosa Cell Tumor, a type of Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors, for which inhibin serves as an important diagnostic marker.

Feature Sertoli-Leydig tumour, Pure Leydig tumour (or Hilus cell tumour) Fibroma, Thecoma, Fibrothecoma Granulosa Cell Tumor Derived from Sertoli or Leydig cells Ovarian stroma Granulosa cells of ovarian follicle Age of Occurrence Second and third decades Any age Postmenopausal (adult type), any age (juvenile type) Associated symptoms Abnormal sexual development or Virilization Associated with Meigs syndrome and basal nevus syndrome Precocious sexual development in juveniles or abnormal uterine bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia (carcinoma) in adults Histological features Reinke crystalloids (in pure Leydig cell tumours) Well-differentiated fibroblasts (fibroma), plump spindle cells with lipid droplets (thecomas) Call-Exner bodies, Coffee bean nuclei (Statement 2) Mutations & Markers Mutations in DICER1 (which encodes endonuclease) Vimentin +, Thecoma: Oil Red O +ve Fibroma: Oil Red O -ve Elevated inhibin levels, CD99+, and FOXL2 mutations (in adult cases) (Statement 4) Prognosis Low recurrence or metastasis rate (<5%) Benign; Rarely malignant (fibrosarcomas) Potentially malignant with unpredictable behaviour; 10-year survival rate 85%

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless testicular mass. An ultrasound shows a well-circumscribed, homogeneous, non-hemorrhagic testicular tumour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The given histopathological image shows features suggestive of testicular seminoma. Histology of seminoma: Sheets of monomorphic cells. The sheets are divided into poorly demarcated lobules by the septa of the fibrous tissue. The septa show lymphocytic infiltration (T lymphocytes). The classic seminoma cell is large and round to polyhedral with a distinct cell membrane and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli.

The cytoplasm is clear or watery appearing and contains glycogen. The arrows in the image below show seminomatous tumour cells. Seminoma: It is the most common germ cell tumour of the testis. A similar presentation in the ovary is called dysgerminoma, and germinoma is present in the pineal gland. Incidence: Peak incidence in the fourth decade.

Genetics: Seminomas contain isochromosome 12p and express OCT3/4 & NANOG. Gross: Seminoma has a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of haemorrhage or necrosis. Generally, the tunica albuginea is not penetrated, but extension to the epididymis, spermatic cord, or scrotal sac occasionally occurs.

questions.question: A patient presents with an ovarian mass that is multiloculated and has a serum CA-125 level >1000 U/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common malignant epithelial ovarian tumour, often bilateral, and tends to be multiloculated with papillary projections. CA-125 is a tumour marker for epithelial ovarian cancers, especially serous and endometrioid types. A very high CA-125 (>1000 U/mL) is far more suggestive of malignancy than benign lesions. Patients often present with abdominal distension, ascites, and an adnexal mass.

**Incorrect Options: Serous cystadenoma (Benign epithelial tumour) (Option A):** Usually unilocular or mildly multilocular, with thin walls and clear serous fluid. CA-125 levels may be normal or only mildly elevated, not usually >1000. There is no invasive growth, and it occurs in younger women compared to cystadenocarcinoma Mature teratoma (Dermoid cyst) (Option B): Benign germ cell tumour containing ectodermal derivatives like hair, teeth, and sebaceous material. It usually occurs in younger women (teens to early adulthood). CA-125 is not a typical marker; instead, you might find elevated AFP or β-hCG in other germ cell tumours (not teratomas). On imaging, it often has fat-fluid levels or calcifications, not a multiloculated cystic appearance.

**Granulosa cell tumour (Sex cord–stromal tumour) (Option C):** Often estrogen-producing may cause precocious puberty in children or postmenopausal bleeding in older women. Serum marker: Inhibin (not CA-125). Usually, a solid or cystic-solid mass, not a multiloculated cyst with such high CA-125.

questions.question: What is the most common site for an extragonadal germ cell tumor?

explanation.text: Extra-gonadal germ cell tumor: The most common site for an extragonadal germ cell tumor is the mediastinum. Extragonadal germ cell tumors can be benign or malignant. Benign extragonadal germ cell tumors are called benign teratomas: These are more common than malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors and are often very large Malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors are divided into two types: Seminoma Non-seminoma

questions.question: The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is the functional unit of the breast. Which of the following is not a part of the TDLU?

explanation.text: Lactiferous ducts are not a part of the TDLU. The morpho-functional unit of the breast is the terminal duct lobular unit(TDLU). TDLU is a grapelike cluster of small alveoli that comprises lobule and terminal duct. A lobule is a collection of multiple ductules, which are epithelial structures that produce milk during lactation. Terminal ducts consist of 2 parts: Intralobular terminal duct: A portion of the terminal duct located within the lobule.
Extralobular terminal duct is the portion connecting the lobule to the lactiferous duct.

questions.question: A 24-year-old with a 2-month-old infant presents to the OPD with pain in her left breast. The baby is exclusively breastfed. On examination, the nipple is tender and erythematous with a fluctuant mass beneath the areola. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario suggests acute breast abscess from lactational mastitis which is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It is caused by a local infection through cracks and fissures in the nipples that occur commonly during the 1st month of breastfeeding. It is often preceded by either engorgement or a focally blocked duct. Patients can develop a focal area of erythema, pain, fever, and swelling.

This can further develop into single or multiple abscesses. Streptococcus pyogenes, Escherichia coli, Bacteroides species, and coagulase-negative Staphylococci are other organisms that cause mastitis.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman presents with pain in her left breast and associated nipple discharge for the past few weeks. She denies any fever, chills, or recent lactation. On examination, a small ovoid, well-defined subareolar mass is felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The patient presenting with breast pain, nipple discharge, and palpable subareolar mass most likely has duct ectasia. Mammary duct ectasia is a benign, non-proliferative breast disease that affects large ducts. It is most common in women who are nearing menopause, typically between the ages of 45 and 55. The breast ducts become clogged with thick secretion and debris, leading to dilation of the duct.

Symptoms Nipple discharge, which can be clear, green, brown, or bloody Breast tenderness or pain, especially around the nipple A tender lump in the subareolar or periareolar region of a breast Inward retraction of the nipple due to repeated episodes and scarring A transverse slit-like or fish-mouth-like retraction of the nipple is classically seen in periductal mastitis but circumferential retraction may indicate a carcinoma.
Ductal ectasia is often diagnosed during a routine mammogram or breast exam and managed by excision. If a lump is found, a biopsy may be needed to rule out cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Zuska’s disease is incorrect?

options.A: There is squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous duct
options.B: Characterized by the formation of keratin plug

explanation.text: Alcohol is a major risk factor in Zuska’s disease along with smoking. Zuska’s disease is also known as Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts(SMOLD), recurrent subareolar abscess, or periductal mastitis. The risk factors include a deficiency of vitamin A associated with smoking(90% of cases). This leads to k eratinizing squamous metaplasia of the ductal epithelium, which is cuboidal. Keratin released from these cells blocks the ductal system.
This leads to the formation of subareolar abscess, dilation, and eventually, the rupture of the duct, causing fistulas.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause a sticky, green, or black discharge from the nipple?

explanation.text: Duct Ectasia: This is a benign (non-cancerous) condition where the milk ducts in the breast widen and thicken. This can cause a blockage and a build-up of fluid, which often appears as a sticky, green, black, or grey discharge from the nipple.

Discharge Colour Disorders Clear or Milky Hormonal fluctuations, Pregnancy, Breastfeeding Yellow, Green, or Brown Duct Ectasia, Infection Bloody Duct Papilloma, Paget's Disease, Breast Cancer White or Cloudy Infection

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a firm, immobile mass in her right breast for the past few days. 2 weeks ago, she bruised her breast while exercising. A mammogram reveals scattered punctate calcifications within the lump. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The most likely diagnosis in this patient with recent trauma and calcification could be fat necrosis. Breast fat necrosis is caused by injured or ischemic breast tissue that is replaced with scar tissue and presents as a palpable nodule. It is commonly caused by breast trauma and breast surgical procedures. It presents as a mammographic density, a painless palpable lump, skin thickening, or deposits of calcium.

Fat necrosis can manifest in a variety of ways that closely resemble cancer like irregular breast mass, usually fixed to the dermis, with possible skin tethering and/or nipple retraction as a result of fibrotic bands between necrotic tissue and skin. Calcifications can sometimes occur in fat necrosis, particularly in older lesions.
These are typically punctate (tiny dots) and scattered throughout the lump, unlike some cancers (differentiated by biopsy).

**Mastitis(Option A):** This is an infection of breast tissue, often caused by bacteria entering through milk ducts during breastfeeding. It can cause inflammation, redness, pain, fever, and chills, which are absent in this case. Breast Abscess(Option B) This is a localized collection of pus within the breast tissue, often caused by a bacterial infection. It presents with fever, chills, and a more fluctuant (fluid-filled) mass compared to the firm mass often felt with fat necrosis.
**Inflammatory Breast Cancer(Option D):** It typically presents with additional symptoms like skin thickening, peau d'orange (skin resembling an orange peel), and rapid progression.

questions.question: What is the absolute risk of a fibrocystic lesion of the breast converting to malignancy?

explanation.text: Fibrocystic disease presents as “lumpy bumpy” breasts on palpation. Patients present with cyclical pain (Pain during menstrual cycle). They are included in the category of non-proliferative breast changes with a relative risk: of 1% and an absolute risk: of 3% of developing invasive carcinoma.

Category Diseases/disorders Relative risk and absolute lifetime risk Non-proliferative breast changes Mild hyperplasia, duct ectasia, cysts, apocrine metaplasia, adenosis, fibroadenoma without complex features Relative risk: 1% Absolute risk: 3% Proliferative diseases without atypia Moderate or florid hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, complex sclerosing lesion, fibroadenoma with complex features Relative risk: 1.5-2% (2%) Absolute risk: 5-7% (6%) Proliferative breast diseases with atypia Atypical ductal hyperplasia Atypical lobular hyperplasia Relative risk: 4-5% (4%) Absolute risk: 13-17% (>12%) Carcinoma in situ Precancerous condition Relative risk: 8-10 (8%) Absolute risk: 25-30% (>24%)

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a firm, irregular mass that has been slowly increasing in size over the past few months. Histopathological examination shows the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical features and HPE showing central sclerosis with fibroelastotic stroma and entrapped glands radiating outwards with hyperplasia are suggestive of radial scar. Radial scars, also known as complex sclerosing lesions, are benign proliferative breast lesions that can mimic breast cancer clinically and radiologically but look like scars when viewed under a microscope.

They are characterized by a spiculated appearance on imaging, with a translucent, low-density center. Grossly, a whitish scar is present at the center (central stellate scar). HPE shows glands entrapped in a hyalinised stroma surrounded by long radiating projections containing epithelium.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with cyclical breast pain, most severe in the week before her period. She also notices her breasts feeling lumpy and swollen around the time of her period, which subsides later. She denies any fever, nipple discharge, or lumps. What is the most likely finding seen in this pathology?

options.A: Peau d'orange appearance of the skin
options.D: Eczematous changes of the nipple and areola

explanation.text: The above features of cyclical pain and breast changes are suggestive of fibrocystic breast disease, which has a blue dome of Bloodgood cyst. Fibrocystic changes of the breast is a benign condition characterized by the development of cysts, fibrosis (thickening and scarring of tissue), and other benign alterations in the breast tissue.

Symptoms Breast pain (mastalgia) or tenderness that fluctuates with menstruation Mastalgia (or mastodynia) can be cyclic (with menses, due to premenstrual edema) or noncyclic (localized to one area of the breast and may be caused by ruptured cysts, physical injury, and infections).

Breast lumps or nodules Swelling or enlargement of the breasts Fluid-filled cysts with varying size Nipple discharge Gross Features: Blue-domed cyst of Bloodgood- Large cysts that contain turbid, semitranslucent brown or blue-colored fluid which imparts a blue color onto the intact cyst. They are typically fluid-filled and may vary in size.

Histopathological Features: Cysts: Fluid-filled sacs within the breast tissue, often surrounded by fibrous tissue. Fibrosis: Thickening and scarring of breast tissue, which may result in palpable lumps or areas of increased density on imaging studies. Apocrine Metaplasia: Transformation of ductal epithelial cells into apocrine-like cells, characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical snouts.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to a mass in her right breast. A 2-cm nodule is noted on breast examination, and the patient is referred for biopsy. Histologic evaluation of the tissue specimen is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The histopathology image shows epithelial ducts compressed and distorted by surrounding stroma which is characteristic of an intracanalicular fibroadenoma. The FNAC features of a fibroadenoma include Staghorn clusters of cells - Ductal cells arranged in a deer horn-like pattern. Bare nuclei - cytoplasm is stripped off and only nuclei are visible in blue color.

Intracanalicular Fibroadenoma: Other features of Fibroadenoma: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically found in women aged 15-35. Spherical masses measuring 1-10 cm, firm, non-tender, well-circumscribed, mobile, and often single. The lump is mobile and slippery and hence called breast mouse. Estrogen sensitivity: Can increase in size during pregnancy, lactation, or estrogen therapy, and usually regress after menopause.

Histopathology: Well-defined borders due to a fibrous capsule, with proliferating stroma potentially compressing and distorting glandular components. Popcorn calcification on mammograms. Aging effect: Epithelium atrophies with age, and the stroma becomes more hyalinized.

Molecular alteration: Alterations in MED12 gene Drug associated with bilateral fibroadenomas: Cyclosporine ( A calcineurin inhibitor) Management: Surgical excision Indications for surgical excision: Age >30 years Size >5 cm Microlobulation on imaging Atypia on histology Family history of breast cancer, and The patient’s preference

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of complex fibroadenoma?

options.C: Nodules of proliferating stroma forming bulbous protrusions

explanation.text: Complex fibroadenoma is an example of epithelial proliferative breast lesions without atypia. Fibroadenoma with complex features has a risk of malignancy, whereas, without complexity, it does not. Complex features include, Cysts > 0.3cm Sclerosing adenosis (sclerosis + increase in the acini cells per lobule i.e, adenosis) Epithelial calcifications Papillary apocrine change (metaplastic change in breast tissue)
